AboutPage.title: About Desmotiva Dev
AboutPage.subtitle: The story behind your daily reality check
AboutPage.metaDescription: Learn about Desmotiva Dev, the project that brings humor and reality to developers. Discover our mission and why healthy demotivation matters.

origin.title: How It All Started
origin.paragraph1: Desmotiva Dev was born from a real need: to bring a bit of humor and reality to developers' daily lives. In a world where we're constantly bombarded with stories of instant success, billion-dollar startups, and developers who learn 5 languages in a weekend, we needed something different.
origin.paragraph2: Created by @deveprogramar, the project started as a way to share the common frustrations every developer faces: inexplicable bugs, impossible legacy code, endless meetings, and that colleague who always breaks the build on Friday at 6pm.
origin.paragraph3: What started as a few funny phrases shared among friends quickly transformed into a community of developers who found comfort in knowing they're not alone in their daily struggles with code.

mission.title: Our Mission
mission.paragraph1: Our mission is simple: to provide a moment of lightness and identification for developers around the world. We believe humor is a powerful tool for dealing with the stress and pressures of a tech career.
mission.paragraph2: We're not here to actually demotivate anyone - quite the opposite. We want to create a space where developers can laugh at the absurd situations we face, recognize that we all go through difficulties, and ultimately feel part of a community that understands.
mission.quote: Sometimes, the best motivation comes from recognizing we're all in the same struggle.

why.title: Why It Matters
why.paragraph1: Tech culture often promotes an unrealistic image of perfection: developers who never make mistakes, code that always works on the first try, and careers that only go up. This constant pressure can lead to burnout, impostor syndrome, and anxiety.
why.paragraph2: Desmotiva Dev offers a necessary counterpoint. By laughing at our common failures and frustrations, we create a healthier and more realistic environment. Benefits include:
why.benefit2: Sense of belonging to a community
why.benefit3: More realistic perspective on tech careers
why.benefit4: Reminders that making mistakes is human and part of the process

creator.title: Who's Behind It
creator.paragraph1: Desmotiva Dev is maintained by @deveprogramar, a developer who, like you, has been through all the situations described in the phrases (and probably some worse ones). With years of experience in software development, he deeply understands the joys and frustrations of the profession.
creator.paragraph2: The project is a love letter to all developers who have ever felt lost, frustrated, or questioned their career choices at 3am while debugging an impossible error.

community.title: Our Community
community.paragraph1: What makes Desmotiva Dev special is the incredible community that has formed around the project. Thousands of developers share the phrases daily, tag their coworkers, and create their own memes based on the content.
community.paragraph2: Whether you're a junior developer struggling with your first project or a senior tired of explaining what Git is for the thousandth time, there's a place for you here. Everyone is welcome to laugh, share, and relate.
community.contribute: Want to contribute your own demotivational phrases? Contact us on Twitter!

post1.title: 10 Signs You Need a Dose of Demotivation
post1.excerpt: Feeling too confident in your code? Think you've finally mastered that technology? Watch out! These are classic signs you need a reality check. Discover the 10 unmistakable signs it's time to visit Desmotiva Dev.
post1.content:
## 1. "It works on my machine"
If this phrase leaves your mouth more than 3 times a week, we have a problem. The client won't access the site from your machine (unless you turn your laptop into a server, which, knowing you, is quite possible).

## 2. You think tests are a "waste of time"
"Why test if I know what I coded?" - said the dev 5 minutes before crashing the production database. Tests aren't there to prove you're right, they're there to prove that you will, invariably, be wrong.

## 3. Your Google history is just Stack Overflow
Don't get me wrong, everyone uses it. But if you need to search "how to declare variable in Python" after 3 years of experience, maybe it's time to rethink.

## 4. You believe the PM's deadline
Ah, sweet innocence. The PM says "just a little button", and you believe it will take 10 minutes. 3 days later, you're refactoring the entire architecture because the button needed a new hardcoded API.

## 5. You dream in code
That's not dedication, that's trauma. If you wake up sweating because you dreamt you forgot a semicolon, you need a vacation (or therapy).

## 6. "I'll comment later"
Spoiler: You won't. Nobody will. That piece of code will stay there, obscure and mysterious, like an Egyptian hieroglyph, until the day someone tries to touch it and curses your descendants.

## 7. Coffee has no effect anymore
If you drink 1 liter of coffee and the only effect is an eyelid twitch, your body has given up. You are powered by anxiety and blown deadlines now.

## 8. Git Push Force is your best friend
If resolving conflicts for you means deleting others' work and imposing your sovereign will on the repository, you're not a leader, you're a bad code dictator.

## 9. You think the user is stupid
The user isn't stupid, they are creative in the art of destroying your software. If your form allows typing a birthdate in the future and the system breaks, it's not the fault of the user born in 2099.

## 10. You are reading this
If you stopped coding to read 10 reasons to get demotivated, congratulations! You have already accepted your fate. Welcome to the club.

post2.title: Anatomy of a Production Bug at 6pm on Friday
post2.excerpt: Every developer knows this moment: it's 5:55pm on Friday, you're about to log out, and then... BOOM! A critical bug in production. Let's explore the complete anatomy of this recurring nightmare and how to survive it (spoiler: you won't).
post2.content:
## 5:55 PM - The False Sense of Security
The sun is setting (lie, you work in a dark room). Slack is getting quiet. You think: "I'll just do this quick deploy, it's just a button color change".

## 5:58 PM - The Fatal Click
`git push origin master`. CI/CD runs. Green lights. You feel like a tech god. Nothing can go wrong. You close your laptop lid.

## 6:02 PM - The Phone Rings
It's not your mom. It's not Uber Eats. It's the CTO. "The site is down. Everything. Even the backup is gone."

## 6:05 PM - Denial
"Impossible, it worked on my machine!", you scream into the void. You frantically open your laptop. Error 500. Error 500 everywhere.

## 6:30 PM - Despair
You discover the "color change" had a cyclic dependency that deleted the users table (don't ask how, you're talented at this). The whole team is summoned. Happy hour is canceled.

## 7:45 PM - The Blame
Someone suggests a rollback. You try. The rollback fails because the database migration wasn't reversible. Of course it wasn't.

## 9:00 PM - The Workaround
Your senior, with deep dark circles, suggests commenting out the line that validates user existence. "Just to get it up", he says. A tear rolls down. The system comes back online, limping, bleeding, but alive.

## 10:15 PM - The Lesson (that won't be learned)
You promise never to deploy on Friday again. You swear on your mechanical keyboard. But we know the truth... Next Friday, at 5:55 PM, the adrenaline will call again.

post3.title: Git Commit Messages: A Story of Desperation
post3.excerpt: From 'fix' to 'IT WORKS DAMMIT' - an epic journey through the most desperate commit messages in software development history. Includes real examples (anonymized to protect the guilty) and tips on how NOT to do it.
post3.content:
## The Beginning: Hope
`feat: adds user authentication`
Look how professional. Conventional Commits standard. Everything beautiful, organized.

## The Middle: Reality
`fix: fixes login bug`
`fix: now it goes`
`fix: fixing typo`
`fix: oh god why doesn't it work`
Here sanity begins to slip through fingers. That cute standard? Gone.

## The End: Chaos
`wip`
`aaaaa`
`WORKS DAMMIT`
`final commit final fr now it goes v2`
`revert "revert "fix: login""`

## Psychiatric Analysis via Git Log
It's possible to trace a dev's psychological profile just by reading their Friday afternoon commits. It starts with stoicism and ends in pure nihilism.

## Golden Tip
If you ever have to `git commit --amend` for the fifth time, stop. Breathe. Go get a coffee. Or accept that your destiny is to have a dirty history forever. After all, "squash commits" at the end only serves to hide the shame, and we know what you did.

post4.title: How to Survive a 2-Hour Daily
post4.excerpt: The daily should last 15 minutes. YOUR daily lasts 2 hours. In this complete guide, we explore survival strategies, meditation techniques during endless meetings, and how to pretend you're paying attention while mentally you're already debugging that error.
post4.content:
## 1. The "Statue" Technique
When the camera is on and you feel sleep hitting, freeze. If someone asks, say your internet froze. Keep your eyes open, but your soul can be sleeping.

## 2. Daily Bingo
Make a mental card:
- "Alignment"
- "Blocker"
- "Synergy"
- "Let's schedule a pre-daily to align the daily"
- "This is legacy's fault"
Whoever completes the card first wins the right to mute the mic and cry.

## 3. The Art of Saying Nothing with Many Words
When it's your turn:
"So, yesterday I had a technical blocker in the API stack, which generated overhead in the deploy throughput, but today I'll act on mitigating this gap to ensure value stream delivery."
Translation: "I did nothing yesterday and I'll do nothing today."

## 4. The Microphone Problem
"Can you hear me?" - repeat this 5 times. "I think my mic is bad, I'll type in chat". There, you won 10 minutes of peace while pretending to fix the sound.

## 5. Productive Dissociation
Learn to make a nodding face while thinking about the grocery list, or why Donald Duck doesn't wear pants but wears a towel when leaving the shower. The important thing is to nod every 30 seconds.

post5.title: Why your code works on your machine (and nowhere else)
post5.excerpt: The phrase "it works on my machine" is the official slogan of the junior developer. Let's find out why the universe conspires against your deploy.
post5.content:
## The Mystical Environment
Your machine is a delicate ecosystem, cultivated with care, where library versions were hand-picked (by chance) and environment variables were hardcoded into the heart of the operating system. The production server, on the other hand, is a hostile wasteland.

## The Curse of Localhost
In localhost, everything is forgiven. The database responds in 0ms, the network never fails, and CORS doesn't exist. It's the Garden of Eden of software. Production is the real world: cruel, slow, and full of firewall rules.

## Phantom Dependencies
Remember that lib you installed globally in 2019 to test a tutorial? Your project depends on it now. Nobody knows, not even you. But the CI/CD server knows. And it will fail the build with sadistic pleasure.

## Would Docker Solve It?
Yes, Docker would solve it. If you knew how to use Docker. But your Dockerfile has more holes than Swiss cheese and the image weighs 4GB because you started from a full Ubuntu instead of Alpine. Now "it works on my machine" became "it works in my container". The problem just changed address.

post6.title: The Art of Writing Comments that Explain Nothing
post6.excerpt: Commenting code is a lost art. Most devs prefer to write the most cryptic code possible and leave it for the next one (or for future self) to decipher.
post6.content:
## The Classic "What"
`i++; // increments i`
Thank you, Captain Obvious. If I didn't know what `++` does, I shouldn't be here. The useless comment takes up space, wastes bytes, and insults the reader's intelligence.

## The Lying Comment
`// Returns true if user is admin`
`return false;`
The code changed. The comment didn't. Now you have a comment that lies blatantly and misleads you. Trust the code, never the comment.

## The Apology
`// God forgive me for this, but the deadline is today`
`eval(input);`
This comment is a cry for help. It doesn't explain the code, it confesses a crime. If you find this, run.

## The Eternal TODO
`// TODO: Refactor this urgent`
(Commit date: 4 years ago)
"Urgent" is a relative concept in software development. This TODO is now part of the system architecture. It's a historical monument.

## The Biography
`// Created by John in 2015. Modified by Mary in 2016. Broken by Peter in 2018.`
Git blame exists for this, people. We don't need a family tree in the file header.

post7.title: Deploy Friday: A Horror Story Based on True Events
post7.excerpt: It was a rainy Friday. The clock struck 4:45 PM. The intern asked: "Can I deploy? It's just a text change". And so the nightmare began.
post7.content:
## The Tragedy Begins
Everyone knows the rule: Friday is read-only day. But human arrogance has no limits. "It's quick", they said. "What could go wrong?", they asked.

## 5:00 PM - The Deploy
The pipeline went green. Success! The team started packing their bags. Slack was quiet. Too quiet.

## 5:15 PM - The First Scream
Support messaged: "Customers can't log in". You think: "Must be cache". Clear cache. Nothing.

## 5:30 PM - The Discovery
The "text change" actually changed the configuration file encoding from UTF-8 to ASCII. All accents became alien characters. The login system crashed when trying to read the username "João".

## 6:00 PM - The Chaos
The rollback failed. The morning backup was corrupted (nobody tested the restore, classic). The CTO is calling. Your pizza got cold. The weekend ended before it began.

## The Lesson
Don't deploy on Friday. It doesn't matter if it's "just text". The universe hates Friday deploys. Respect the IT gods or pay with your sanity.

FAQPage.title: Frequently Asked Questions
FAQPage.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Desmotiva Dev

q1.question: What is Desmotiva Dev?
q1.answer: Desmotiva Dev is a humor project aimed at developers and tech professionals. We offer funny demotivational phrases that reflect the real situations and frustrations of daily programming work. Our goal is to bring lightness and identification through humor, creating a community where developers can laugh at the common difficulties of the profession.

q2.question: Are the phrases really meant to demotivate?
q2.answer: No! Despite the name, the goal is not to demotivate anyone. Actually, it's the opposite: by laughing at the absurd situations and common frustrations we all face, we create a sense of community and belonging. Humor is a healthy way to deal with the stress and pressure of a tech career. Think of it as a well-humored 'reality check'.

q3.question: How can I use the phrases?
q3.answer: You can freely use the phrases to share with friends, coworkers, or on social media. Just click the 'Generate Phrase' button to receive a random phrase, then you can copy or share directly on WhatsApp, Twitter, or LinkedIn. We only ask that when sharing, you mention Desmotiva Dev or use the hashtag #desmotivadev to help more people discover the project.

q4.question: Can I contribute my own phrases?
q4.answer: Yes! We love receiving contributions from the community. If you have a funny demotivational phrase about programming or development situations, contact us through Twitter (@deveprogramar). We evaluate all suggestions and, if approved, they can be added to the phrase generator with proper credits.

q5.question: Is the site free?
q5.answer: Yes, Desmotiva Dev is completely free to use. We don't charge anything and never will. The site is maintained through Google AdSense ads, which help us cover hosting and maintenance costs. Our goal is to keep the project accessible to all developers.

q6.question: Do you have an API?
q6.answer: We currently don't have a public API available, but it's something we're considering for the future. If you're interested in integrating Desmotiva Dev phrases into your project, contact us to discuss possibilities.

q7.question: How can I report a problem or bug?
q7.answer: If you found a technical problem on the site or have improvement suggestions, please contact us through Twitter (@deveprogramar). We also accept issues on GitHub if the repository is public. We highly value community feedback and constantly work to improve the experience.

q8.question: Can I use the phrases commercially?
q8.answer: The phrases are created for personal use and social media sharing. For commercial use (such as in products, merchandising, or commercial publications), please contact us first to discuss terms and obtain proper authorization.

q9.question: Do you have presence on other social networks?
q9.answer: Currently, our main presence is on Twitter through the @deveprogramar account. That's where we share updates, new phrases, and interact with the community. We're considering expanding to other platforms in the future, so stay tuned!

q10.question: How often are new phrases added?
q10.answer: We're constantly working to add new phrases to the database. We currently have over 75 phrases and add new ones regularly, especially when we receive good contributions from the community. Our goal is to keep the content always fresh and relevant.

q11.question: Does the site collect my personal data?
q11.answer: We don't collect personally identifiable information. We use Google Analytics to understand how visitors use the site (anonymous data like pages visited, time spent, etc.) and Google AdSense to display ads. For more details, see our complete Privacy Policy.

q12.question: Can I suggest improvements to the site?
q12.answer: Absolutely! We love hearing suggestions from the community. If you have ideas for new features, design improvements, or any other suggestion, contact us on Twitter. All suggestions are welcome and carefully considered.
